note: Luke opens with a single long, carefully balanced sentence in polished literary Greek, the kind that began histories and medical treatises of the day. He admits that **many** before him have written accounts ({lk 1:1 πολλοὶ ἐπεχείρησαν}, *polloi epecheirēsan*, “many have undertaken”) and promises to write {lk 1:3 ἀκριβῶς καθεξῆς} (*akribōs kathexēs*, “carefully, in order”). Most scholars think Mark was one of those “many” accounts; on the early church's view that Matthew wrote first, Matthew would be among them. Right after this preface, Luke's Greek shifts into a Semitic, Septuagint-like style.

Where Mark begins at the Jordan, Matthew with Abraham and Luke with a temple priest, John starts before creation: {jn 1:1 Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος} (*en archē ēn ho logos*, “in the beginning was the Word”), echoing the first words of Genesis in Greek. In {jn 1:14 ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν} the verb is *eskēnōsen*, literally “pitched his tent among us”, recalling the tabernacle where God's glory lived in Israel's wilderness years.

The two genealogies share almost no wording; the computed overlap is only a few percent. Matthew runs **forward** from Abraham with a steady refrain, {mt 1:2 Ἀβραὰμ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Ἰσαάκ} (“Abraham fathered Isaac”). Luke runs **backward** from Jesus to “Adam, son of God” in a chain of genitives, {lk 3:23 τοῦ Ἠλὶ} (“of Heli”), and names a different grandfather for Joseph. Both pause at the same point: Jesus is Joseph's son {lk 3:23 ὡς ἐνομίζετο} (“as was supposed”). The two lines have long been reconciled: many read Luke's as Mary's line, and Julius Africanus (3rd century) explained the difference by levirate marriage.

Luke's narrative opens in the temple, with an elderly childless couple who deliberately echo Abraham and Sarah. The Greek here suddenly reads like the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament: clauses strung together with “and”, and Hebrew-style turns such as *egeneto* (“and it came to pass”). Many scholars think Luke deliberately imitated biblical style so that the story of Jesus begins as a continuation of Israel's scriptures. This material is found only in Luke.

Gabriel's greeting {lk 1:28 Χαῖρε κεχαριτωμένη} (*chaire kecharitōmenē*) is a pun in Greek: *chaire*, the ordinary word for “hello” (literally “rejoice”), shares its root with *charis*, “grace/favor”. The second word is a perfect participle meaning “one who has been favored”. Luke tells the story from Mary's side, where Matthew's birth story is told from Joseph's. The two accounts share almost no wording.

Mary's song is woven almost entirely from Old Testament phrases, especially Hannah's prayer in 1 Samuel 2. Its first word, {lk 1:46 Μεγαλύνει} (*megalynei*, “magnifies”), gives it its Latin name. Its central theme, God lowering the powerful and lifting the lowly, recurs throughout Luke: the poor, women and outsiders get more attention in this Gospel than in any other.

Zechariah's hymn (the *Benedictus*) closes the birth of John the Baptist with Israel-centered hopes: deliverance from enemies, covenant, the oath to Abraham. Luke builds his first two chapters in **pairs**: two annunciations, two births, two hymns, John always the forerunner and Jesus the greater. None of this appears in any other Gospel, and the Greek is again heavily Septuagint-flavored.

Matthew tells the birth through Joseph's dreams and introduces his signature device, the “fulfillment formula”: {mt 1:22 ἵνα πληρωθῇ τὸ ῥηθὲν ὑπὸ κυρίου διὰ τοῦ προφήτου} (“to fulfill what the Lord had spoken through the prophet”). He quotes Isaiah 7:14 from the Greek Septuagint, whose {mt 1:23 ἡ παρθένος} (*hē parthenos*, “the virgin”) renders a Hebrew word (*almah*) that means “young woman”, a difference much discussed ever since. Traditional readers note that the Jewish translators of the Septuagint themselves chose *parthenos*, two centuries before Jesus.

Luke anchors the birth in imperial history with a census decree of Augustus, a dating that historians find hard to square with other sources. Defenders of Luke's accuracy propose an earlier enrollment under Augustus, or read {lk 2:2 πρώτη} as “before” the census of Quirinius. The famous {lk 2:7 ἐν τῷ καταλύματι} (*katalyma*) is the same word Luke later uses for the “guest room” of the Last Supper, so “no room in the guest room” may be closer than “no room at the inn”. The angels' title {lk 2:11 σωτὴρ ὅς ἐστιν χριστὸς κύριος} (“a Savior, who is Christ the Lord”) uses titles that were also claimed by the emperor.

The infant Jesus is brought to the temple, where two aged prophets, Simeon and Anna, a man and a woman, recognize him. Luke often pairs male and female figures this way. Simeon's *Nunc Dimittis* adds a note that runs through Luke and Acts: salvation as “a light for revelation to the Gentiles.” Only Luke places Jesus in the Jerusalem temple as a child, and his Gospel will also end in the temple.

Only Matthew has the magi: Persian or Babylonian star-watchers, not “kings” (that tradition came later). Gentile outsiders come to worship while Jerusalem's king plots murder, previewing Matthew's ending, where the risen Jesus sends his disciples to “all nations”. Matthew again cites scripture (Micah 5:2) to locate the birth in Bethlehem.

Matthew models this story on Moses: a tyrant kills infant boys, the child escapes, and he returns when “those seeking the child's life are dead” (wording borrowed from Exodus 4:19 in the Septuagint). The quotation {mt 2:15 Ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ἐκάλεσα τὸν υἱόν μου} (“Out of Egypt I called my son”) applies Hosea's words about Israel to Jesus, a typical move in Matthew, who presents Jesus as reliving Israel's story.

The only story about Jesus between infancy and adulthood in the canonical Gospels. His first recorded words are {lk 2:49 ἐν τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου δεῖ εἶναί με}, literally “I must be in the things of my Father”. The Greek leaves the place unspecified (“house” or “affairs”), and translations differ. Luke's {lk 2:49 δεῖ} (*dei*, “it is necessary”) is a word he uses throughout for the divine plan.

Mark introduces John with a quotation he attributes to {mk 1:2 ἐν τῷ Ἠσαΐᾳ τῷ προφήτῃ} (“in Isaiah the prophet”), but its first half actually comes from Malachi 3:1. **Both** Matthew and Luke keep the Isaiah line and drop the Malachi words here (Matthew uses them later, at 11:10). Luke also sets the scene with a formal six-part date, the fifteenth year of Tiberius, the way a Greek historian would.

A run of **24 consecutive identical Greek words** between Matthew and Luke, and over 80% agreement in all. Since Mark lacks this speech, it is a prime exhibit for “Q”, the proposed lost source of sayings; on the Farrer view, Luke copied it from Matthew. The audience differs: in Matthew John attacks {mt 3:7 τῶν Φαρισαίων καὶ Σαδδουκαίων} (“Pharisees and Sadducees”), in Luke the crowds.

Only Luke has John answer practical questions from the crowds, toll collectors and soldiers: {lk 3:10 Τί οὖν ποιήσωμεν} (“What then should we do?”). The answers are about money and possessions: share a spare tunic, collect no more than you're owed, don't extort. That fits Luke's lasting interest in wealth and the poor. The same question returns, word for word, in Acts 2:37.

This unit has 27 “minor agreements”, places where Matthew and Luke agree against Mark. Most striking is that both add {mt 3:11 καὶ πυρί} (“and with fire”) to Mark's “he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit”, and both continue with the winnowing fork, which Mark lacks. Two-Source scholars see Mark and Q overlapping here; Farrer scholars see Luke following Matthew.

In Mark the heavens are {mk 1:10 σχιζομένους} (*schizomenous*, “being torn apart”), a violent verb Mark uses again only when the temple curtain is torn at Jesus' death. Matthew and Luke both soften it to “opened”, one of the minor agreements. Mark and Luke keep the voice private, {mk 1:11 Σὺ εἶ ὁ υἱός μου} (“**You** are my Son”); Matthew makes it a public announcement, {mt 3:17 Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μου} (“**This** is my Son”).

Mark's version is two verses, and blunt: the Spirit {mk 1:12 ἐκβάλλει} (*ekballei*, “drives out”, the verb used for exorcisms) Jesus into the wilderness. Matthew and Luke both soften this to “led” and both add a three-part dialogue with the devil, sharing much of its wording. They put the temptations in a different order: Matthew ends on a mountain, Luke at the Jerusalem temple, his Gospel's center of gravity.

Here John's first disciples come from the Baptist's circle in Judea, not from fishing boats in Galilee as in the other Gospels. John is the only evangelist to keep Aramaic titles and translate them: {jn 1:41 τὸν Μεσσίαν ὅ ἐστιν μεθερμηνευόμενον χριστός} (“the Messiah, which is translated Christ”), and *Kēphas* explained as *Petros*, “rock”. In John, Jesus is openly named Messiah on the first pages; in Mark it is a secret until halfway through.
